title: The page behind the screen
insertion: After AIR Cuttack, before Parbati Ghose, Part I
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
chapter_markdown:
A page can hold a voice before a camera finds a face for it. In Odisha’s storytelling, the journey from writing to performance is often a change of company: a narrator gives way to actors, musicians, technicians and an audience. The words do not travel alone.

## Reading the place we live in

In the chapter “Bhagia and Saria” of ଛମାଣ ଆଠଗୁଣ୍ଠ (Chha Mana Atha Guntha), Fakir Mohan Senapati’s narrator turns towards educated readers who know distant societies better than their neighbours. The question is deliberately ironic:

“ଆପଣାର ବା ପ୍ରତିବାସୀ ଜାତି ଓ ସମାଜର କଥା ଜାଣିବାର ଦରକାର କ'ଣ ?”

“What need is there to know about our own community and society, or our neighbours’?”

English rendering for this edition. The narrator’s apparent dismissal is a rebuke to that indifference.[^lit-neighbours]

The passage offers Project Odisha a useful question about its own work. What do we learn to notice when we look closely at a place? A history of cinema can follow famous careers and prizes while also attending to the labour, speech and unequal relationships that stories make visible. Knowing a region is not the same as praising everything within it.

Parbati Ghose’s 1986 film carries this novel into the cinema; her chapter later in this book follows the adaptation’s credited makers.[^lit-parbati] Reading the novel beside the film invites questions rather than a verdict of fidelity. What can an actor convey without the narrator’s explanation? Where might a pause, a gesture or a cut carry the work of a sentence? These are invitations to comparison, not descriptions of scenes we have established from the film.

## Before the screen, an act of listening

In the opening household passage of ରେବତୀ (Rebati), Fakir Mohan describes a child beside her father as he reads and sings:

“ରେବତୀ ପାଖରେ ବସି ଶୁଣୁଥାଏ।”

“Rebati would sit beside him and listen.”

English rendering for this edition.[^lit-rebati]

This short excerpt makes listening part of a child’s learning. It belongs to a literary household, not a record of a particular film production. Read alongside the AIR Cuttack chapter, it invites us to consider different settings in which a voice gathers listeners: beside a family member, around a radio, inside a cinema. The comparison is ours; it does not claim that this passage caused a broadcasting or film tradition.

The medium changes who can hear, when they can hear, and whether they can answer. A radio performance cannot rely on a face being visible. A film can hold on a face while speech falls away. Literature can let a narrator interrupt both the action and the reader’s confidence. Each makes room for a different kind of attention.

## Stories that return in another form

There are concrete adaptation paths through the book. କା (Kaa) carries Kanhucharan Mohanty’s novel into film; the Gour–Parbati archive identifies the source and the directing collaboration.[^lit-kaa] ଭୂଖା (Bhukha) grew from Manglu Charan Biswal’s play, placing the livelihood of folk performers within a Sambalpuri screen story.[^lit-bhukha] ପ୍ରତୀକ୍ଷା (Pratikshya) draws on Gourahari Das’s story, a connection described in the cast-and-crew account at IFFI.[^lit-pratikshya] The official publicity for ଅନନ୍ତା (Ananta) identifies Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Randi Pua Ananta as its literary source.[^lit-ananta]

These connections should not be flattened into one timeless regional style. A novel, a play and a short story offer different ways of arranging people and events. Sambalpuri speech and performance carry their own local relationships. A new adaptation also belongs to the time in which it is made: to its actors, its audience and the practical circumstances of production.

## Carrying the words forward

The literary connection can become a reading path rather than a decorative quotation. Read a source passage, watch the available film or official excerpt, and compare a specific decision: who speaks, whose point of view is retained, and what the new form leaves unsaid. Keep the writer’s and translator’s names beside the words. A borrowed line should bring its context with it.

For Project Odisha, the page and the screen can therefore lead readers back to one another. A film may draw someone towards a writer; a story may send someone looking for a performance. The task is to keep those doors open, with sources that can be found and voices that remain distinct.

book_only_poetic_additions.text: A film has more than one lifetime. There is the time lived by its characters, the time spent making it, and the later years in which its images must survive. The restoration story asks us to hold all three together.
A drumbeat can carry a gathering; it cannot, by itself, settle what the drummer will earn. Listening closely means making room for both the sound and the life that sustains it.
The microphone holds no visible audience. Yet the work behind it reaches towards someone listening elsewhere. That distance is part of radio’s intimacy: a public voice arriving in a private room.
